# International Expansion — Entry & Establishment Strategy
## Version 2 (complete; for Board decision at Gate 0)

**Company:** Mid-sized sustainable apparel brand, established in Western Europe
**Prepared by:** Growth working group, with Sourcing, Finance and Legal
**Circulated to:** CEO · CFO · Brand & Product Director · Sourcing Director · Head of Digital · Head of Legal · Head of Sustainability · Board

**Status.** A recommendation, with a specific ask (§16). Version 1 was reviewed and found to be an unfinished paper that answered one of the three questions asked, and that rested a sequencing decision on an unexamined duty assumption. Both criticisms were correct, and one of them reverses our recommendation. We are grateful for the correction; it is far cheaper here than at Gate 2.

**Figures marked *illustrative*** are shape, to be confirmed with Finance, a customs adviser and the market. They are given so the size of the commitment is visible, not because we are confident in them. **All duty and tariff positions in this paper are a strategic reading and require written confirmation from a customs adviser before Gate 1.**

---

## 0. What changed from Version 1, and why

We record this so colleagues who commented can see their guidance carried through.

| Change | Reason |
|---|---|
| **1. Sequence inverted: Türkiye is now the first supply move, India the second.** | The landed-cost arithmetic was not modelled. Türkiye enters the EU duty-free under the customs union; Indian apparel pays MFN duty in the ~12% band, with 5–6 weeks of sea freight and the working capital that consumes. That is a materially different answer, and it was ours to check before recommending. §3, §6. |
| **2. EU–Japan EPA now claimed, and the "hinge" re-priced.** | EU-origin goods enter Japan duty-free under the EPA. India-made goods do not qualify. The hinge was presented as a free option; the origin arithmetic decides its value. §6.3. |
| **3. Two screens, not one.** | Ranking Japan on "supply fit" was a category error against our own §1 argument. §2 now runs a demand screen and a supply screen separately, with the weighted arithmetic shown. |
| **4. A marketing plan now exists (§8), with channel splits, CAC/LTV assumptions and a trade calendar.** | Version 1 had four bullets. The brief asked for channels; we did not answer it. |
| **5. Operational steps now exist (§9), led by trademark filing in Month 0.** | Japan is first-to-file and apparel squatting is routine. Filing before any agent conversation, listing or press. Its absence was a straightforward error. |
| **6. Numbers (§11): revenue, working capital, unit economics, break-even, cash-at-risk.** | Asking the Board for sight while giving it nothing to size is not a modest paper, it is an unusable one. |
| **7. Australia/NZ added and seriously considered; Canada, Nordics/CEE, USA dismissed on the record.** | Counter-seasonality is a genuine inventory-risk answer for a brand our size. Its omission was a gap, not a judgement. |
| **8. Organic cotton certification integrity promoted to its own workstream (§10.1); competitor map added (§7); our own Scope 3 credibility addressed (§10.5).** | Each is brand-lethal for a claims-led business and each was buried in a scorecard cell. |
| **9. Register corrected.** | "This paper does not tell anyone what to do" was inherited from a crisis playbook and was abdication dressed as courtesy. This paper does recommend. Caveats now attach to specific numbers, where they belong. |

---

## 1. The question behind the question

The brief asks for one region delivering new customers *and* new manufacturing. That is two questions wearing one coat.

The geographies where premium sustainable apparel commands a price are, with few exceptions, not the geographies where it is competitively made. Forcing both onto one map produces a compromise that is second-best at each: a factory base in a market that cannot afford the product, or a demand beachhead with no supply logic behind it.

We therefore separate the vectors and look for where they *touch*:

- **Demand** — where are there latent buyers who will pay for the proposition?
- **Supply** — where can we make it better, more traceably, and with a second source we do not currently have?
- **The hinge** — is there a region where a supply base can, over time, also serve regional demand? "Make in region, sell in region" is where the margin sits and where the carbon story stops being a slide. §6.3 tests whether the hinge survives its own duty arithmetic.

**Our real starting asset.** We are single-sourced, EU-concentrated, and carrying a regulatory apparatus (CSRD, CSDDD, Green Claims / Empowering Consumers, ESPR and Digital Product Passport, textile EPR) that we have treated as cost. That apparatus is a traceability and substantiation capability almost no competitor in our size class has built. Our export may not be the clothing.

---

## 2. Screening — two screens, arithmetic shown

Version 1's single scorecard contradicted §1. Corrected: demand markets are screened on demand criteria, supply markets on supply criteria. Weights are chosen for a mid-sized balance sheet, i.e. weighted toward **reversibility**.

### 2.1 Demand screen

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Segment paying a premium for provenance/quality | 25% |
| Channel access for an unknown foreign brand | 20% |
| Reversibility of entry (wholesale/marketplace before entity) | 20% |
| Claim-substantiation and litigation risk (inverse) | 15% |
| Operating friction (entity, tax, labelling, payments, FX) | 10% |
| Inventory-risk relief (counter-seasonality, off-price channel) | 10% |

Scores 1–5, *illustrative*, weighted total to one decimal:

| Market | Premium 25% | Channel 20% | Revers. 20% | Claim risk 15% | Friction 10% | Inventory 10% | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Japan** | 5 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 2 | **4.05** |
| **Australia / NZ** | 4 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 5 | **4.15** |
| **South Korea** | 4 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **3.65** |
| **USA (East Coast)** | 4 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2 | **3.10** |
| **Canada** | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **3.05** |
| **UAE / Gulf** | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3 | **3.45** |

Corrections we accept from review, visible in the numbers above: **Japan's duty position is a 4, not a 3** (EU–Japan EPA, §6.3). **The USA's reversibility is a 4, not a 2** — wholesale and specialist e-tail entry there is genuinely reversible, and Version 1's score was bent to fit its conclusion. The USA is still not first, but for the honest reasons: acquisition cost against a mature, well-funded domestic sustainable cohort, and a claims-litigation environment in a category of its own. That is a claim-risk argument, and it is now scored as one.

**Australia/NZ now scores marginally ahead of Japan** and was missing from Version 1 altogether. English-language, low friction, high willingness-to-pay, and — the point that matters for a brand carrying our inventory risk — **counter-seasonal**, which converts end-of-season European stock from a markdown problem into a full-margin channel. We do not, however, recommend it as the *beachhead* (§3), and the reason should be stated plainly rather than hidden in the scorecard: the market is shallow, it credentials us nowhere else, and a scorecard that rewards ease will always over-reward it. Judgement overrides the model here, and we would rather say so than adjust a weight until the model agrees with us. **Canada** is dismissed as a US derivative better entered after the US. **Nordics/CEE** is home-region deepening, not expansion, and belongs in the core plan.

### 2.2 Supply screen

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Landed cost into EU (FOB + duty + freight + WC carry) | 30% |
| Capability at our quality and certification standard | 20% |
| Certification and claim integrity (verifiable chain of custody) | 20% |
| Speed / replenishment and audit accessibility | 15% |
| Country and FX stability | 10% |
| Headroom to grow with us; are we a good customer? | 5% |

| Source | Landed 30% | Capability 20% | Integrity 20% | Speed 15% | Stability 10% | Headroom 5% | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Türkiye** | 5 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 3 | **4.30** |
| **India** | 3 | 5 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 5 | **3.25** |
| **Portugal (incumbent-adjacent)** | 3 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 2 | **4.15** |
| **Vietnam** | 4 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 4 | 2 | **3.70** |
| **Bangladesh** | 5 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | **3.35** |

**This is the reversal.** Türkiye's landed-cost score is not a preference, it is the customs union: duty-free entry, 3–5 week replenishment, GOTS-certified capacity, and a two-hour flight for unannounced audits. India's capability and headroom are the best on the board — fibre-to-garment depth, artisan capability that is defensible as *product* rather than as story — but it carries ~12% MFN duty into the EU, 5–6 weeks of sea freight, the working capital that lead time consumes, and the certification-integrity exposure in §10.1. Version 1 called Türkiye a "hedge." On the arithmetic it is the first move.

**Bangladesh** scores best on cost and worst where we cannot afford to score badly. The LDC graduation timetable removes the duty advantage inside our planning horizon, and it substitutes one single-country concentration for another.

**Portugal** is included deliberately, and it scores second. Before we cross a continent, the Board is entitled to ask whether deepening and diversifying within our existing supply geography answers the sourcing half of the brief at a fraction of the risk. Our answer is that it answers resilience but not cost or growth headroom — but it is a legitimate alternative to the whole of Vector B, and §15 treats it as one.

---

## 3. The recommendation — three vectors, re-sequenced

| Vector | Where | Why | Horizon |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Demand beachhead** | **Japan**, Tokyo-first | Pays for material quality, longevity and repair without needing to be lectured. Wholesale and department-store structures let an unknown brand be validated by an intermediary the customer already trusts. **EU-origin goods enter duty-free under the EPA.** Deep, patient, and it credentials us across Asia. | Months 0–18 |
| **B1 — Supply, first move** | **Türkiye** (Aegean/İzmir, İstanbul) | Duty-free into the EU, 3–5 week replenishment, GOTS capacity, auditable on a two-hour flight. **Cheaper landed, faster, and EU-compliance-native.** Learn second-sourcing here, where mistakes are recoverable. | Months 0–12 |
| **B2 — Supply, deeper** | **India** — knits Tiruppur/Coimbatore, wovens Bengaluru/NCR, artisan Rajasthan/Gujarat | Fibre-to-garment depth, growth headroom, and craft capability that becomes product. Held to **Gate 2**, conditional on the certification-integrity workstream (§10.1) passing and on our order book clearing quality-mill MOQs (§10.2). | Months 12–30 |
| **Counter-seasonal channel** | **Australia / NZ**, wholesale-only | Not a beachhead — an inventory instrument. Two agents, no entity, no marketing spend, taking EU end-of-season at full local margin. Cheap, reversible, and it funds part of Vector A. | Months 6–18 |
| **The hinge** | India, later, **only if §6.3 clears** | India-made, Asia-sold. Shortest freight, cleanest carbon arithmetic we will ever have — but India-origin goods forfeit EPA preference into Japan. We buy the option only when the origin arithmetic is written down. | Month 30+ |

**Why this sequence and not Version 1's.** A generates price validation and the story; B1 generates margin, speed and a second source immediately and cheaply; the Australian channel absorbs inventory risk that would otherwise sit against A's launch; B2 is the growth engine, entered once we know how to run a second source at all. Version 1 ran A and B(India) in parallel and asserted they made each other cheaper. On the evidence they share almost no infrastructure in the first eighteen months, and the assertion was unearned. Türkiye and Japan *do* share something real: both are served by the same EU-origin production base, and EPA preference depends on it.

**Bandwidth.** Three moves, one continent-crossing deferred. The resourcing plan is in §11.4. If the honest answer at Gate 0 is that we have capacity for two moves rather than three, drop the Australian channel — it is the most reversible and the least strategic. Do not drop B1, and do not accelerate B2 to compensate.

---

## 4. Entry mode — light footprint, high learning

Distributor versus subsidiary is a question of *stage*, not philosophy.

**Japan, Phase 1 (Months 0–12).**
- **Commercial agent, not exclusive distributor.** Commission-remunerated; exclusivity limited to 12 months and to named accounts; performance-linked renewal. Exclusivity given away cheaply in month two is how brands lose a decade in Japan.
- **Marketplace in parallel** — ZOZOTOWN and/or Rakuten Fashion for demand signal and size-curve data. Commission is material (*illustrative: 25–35%*). Treat as paid research with revenue attached, not as the channel.
- **Own D2C** properly localised: Japanese-language site, JPY pricing, credit/konbini/PayPay/Rakuten Pay, domestic returns address, **LINE as primary CRM** rather than email.
- **One hire before any of it**: a senior, local Japan Market Lead with a wholesale rolodex. One excellent person and no office beats an office and a coordinator.

**Japan, Phase 2 (from Gate 2).** *Kabushiki Kaisha* or branch; 3PL in Chiba/Kanagawa; a controlled pop-up or shop-in-shop before any lease. Tokyo physical retail is a marketing instrument with a rent bill — bought when the brand can fill it, not to make the brand exist.

**Türkiye (supply).** Direct vendor relationships from the outset; no agent. Two mills minimum per product family. A retained local QC/compliance inspector (part-time, *illustrative €3–4k/month*) rather than an office. Written FOB pricing in EUR, not USD, to keep FX exposure where we can see it.

**India (from Gate 2).** Buying agent for months 0–9 of that phase to compress the search, replaced by our **own sourcing liaison office** by month 12 — the agent's incentive is order volume, ours is chain-of-custody integrity, and those diverge quietly.

**Australia/NZ.** Two commission agents, wholesale-only, no entity, no local stockholding beyond consignment. If it fails, it costs a season of samples.

**What we avoid.** A JV we do not need for market access; a licence that puts our name on product we do not control; an acquisition of a local brand before we can value it.

---

## 5. Product positioning

"Sustainable" does not translate. It localises, or it fails. **These claims are our working hypotheses, not findings — Gate 1 is contingent on the validation in §12.1 testing them.**

| Market | What the proposition is *about* | What to keep quiet |
|---|---|---|
| **Western Europe (home)** | Certified, circular, transparent — an ethical purchase | — |
| **Japan** | **Longevity, material honesty, quiet craft.** Fabric weight, seam construction, repair service, "one you keep for ten years". Environmental credentials as *evidence of care* — in the footnote, not the headline. | Moralising. Loud activism. Volume claims about CO₂ saved: immodest, and it invites verification we may not survive. |
| **Australia / NZ** | Durability for an outdoor climate; provenance stated plainly | European superiority of any kind |
| **South Korea (wave 2)** | **Design credibility with a conscience attached.** Silhouette first, story second, social proof throughout. | Slow-fashion sermons in a market moving in six-week cycles. |
| **Gulf (watch)** | Quality, modest-adaptable cut, discretion | Lifestyle instruction |

**Product architecture — 70/20/10.**
- **70% carry-over core**, unchanged: protects margin and brand coherence.
- **20% regional adaptation** — the unglamorous work: sizing down one to two increments with revised sleeve and inseam for Japan; lighter fabric weights for humid summers; a rainy-season capsule; colour palettes reset from Northern E…[truncated]

# Crisis Response & Reputation Recovery — Operating Strategy
## Version 4 (revised following review)

**Document type:** Operating playbook. Part A is intended to be usable in the first hour without being read in full.
**Prepared by:** International Brand Risk working group, with the market team
**Circulated to:** Regional President (market) · Market General Manager · Group Chief Marketing Officer · Group General Counsel · Group Communications · Group Head of Security · Group Finance / Investor Relations · Group HR · Group Internal Audit
**Status:** A proposal for endorsement, offered with respect. Colleagues closer to the market, and colleagues with legal and financial responsibility, will see things the working group cannot. Where this document is wrong, we would be grateful to be corrected before it is needed rather than during.
**Figures marked *illustrative*** are placeholders to be confirmed with Finance and the market team; they are included so that the shape of the commitment is visible, not because we have any confidence in the numbers.

---

## 0. Note on this revision

The previous draft was reviewed and found, quite rightly, to be an essay rather than an instrument. We are grateful for the correction. Six things have changed, and we record them here so that colleagues who commented can see their guidance reflected:

1. The response now has **three settings, not one**. Unconditional maximum response was itself a risk; a national on-camera apology delivered against a few hundred coordinated accounts manufactures the crisis it was meant to answer.
2. **Global withdrawal is now a decision rule, not an instruction.** The earlier circularity — withdrawing globally to prevent contagion, when the withdrawal itself is the contagion vector — has been removed.
3. The **legal posture has been rewritten**. The recommendation to publish individual approval accountability has been withdrawn entirely. We publish the failure of *process*; we never publish *people*. Where our first draft treated legal exposure as generally overstated, we accept that in markets with religious-insult, national-symbol or criminal-defamation regimes the exposure falls personally on the local country manager, and that this is not ours to accept on his or her behalf.
4. **Safety, welfare and spokesperson protection** have been added. Their absence was a straightforward failure of care, and the working group regrets it.
5. A **commercial section** now exists — cost envelope, insurance notification, agency indemnity, investor materiality test.
6. The **five internal tensions** identified in review are reconciled in §17 rather than left to be argued in the room at hour three.

The diagnosis that the reviewer was kind about has been compressed and moved to Annex A. It matters, but not in the first hour.

---

# PART A — THE FIRST 72 HOURS

## 1. Action grid

Owners are given by role. **Default names should be entered before this document is filed**, and confirmed by the Regional President; an unnamed owner is an unowned action. Times are from **T0 = the moment the market team judges the reaction to be more than routine comment**, not from the moment senior management is informed.

| By | Action | Owner (R) | Consulted / Informed |
|---|---|---|---|
| T+30 min | Open incident log (single timestamped file, assume it will be disclosed one day). Convene pod on standing bridge. | Market Comms Lead | Pod |
| T+1 hr | **Freeze**: suspend all scheduled in-market activity — paid, organic, promotional, influencer, executive appearances, launches. Reversible, requires no approval. | Market Marketing Director | Media agency, Group CMO (informed) |
| T+1 hr | Notify Group Comms, Group GC, Regional President by pre-agreed one-page alert (Annex D template). No analysis, no reassurance. | Market GM | Group |
| T+2 hrs | Preliminary **safety assessment** (§6): offices, stores, distribution points, community managers, agency staff. | Group Security, with Market HR | Market GM |
| T+3 hrs | Instruct **local cultural counsel** (external, retained in advance where possible) and independent local research partner. | Market GM | Pod |
| T+4 hrs | Community managers switched to holding protocol: acknowledge, do not argue, never mock, do not mass-delete, escalate threats. | Digital / Community Lead | Market Comms Lead |
| T+6 hrs | **Reaction verification read** (§5): unique authors vs. reposts, geographic concentration, authenticity indicators, political or competitive sponsorship. First tier assignment. | Insights / Social Listening Lead | Pod decides tier |
| T+6 hrs | Legal exposure screen: statutory, criminal, regulatory, personal-liability. Written, specific, one page. | Market Counsel + Group GC | Pod |
| T+8 hrs | Brief customer service, store and call-centre staff. Permission to say "we got this wrong" without a script. Abuse-reporting route opened. | Market Customer Service Lead | Market HR |
| T+8 hrs | Direct contact — voice, not mailshot — with top retail, distribution and franchise partners. | Market Sales Director | Market GM |
| T+10 hrs | Internal note to all market employees, written as if it will be external, because it will be. | Market GM + Market HR | Group HR |
| T+12 hrs | Withdrawal decision under §4 rule. In-market withdrawal executed; global position set (withdraw / freeze / hold). | Market GM proposes; Group CMO ratifies within 2 hrs or default applies | Group Comms, Group GC |
| T+12 hrs | Apology **form** selected under §9 overlay (statement / on-camera / institutional / in-person / physical gesture). | Market GM with cultural counsel | Group Comms (informed) |
| T+18 hrs | Insurance notification opened (§8). Time-barred provisions checked. | Market Finance Lead | Group Risk & Insurance |
| T+24 hrs | **Holding statement published** (Annex B, tiered drafts). Local language first, English second. Three elements only: unqualified acknowledgement of hurt; confirmation of withdrawal; date by which a fuller response will come. | Market GM / spokesperson per tier | Pod |
| T+24 hrs | Forensic review of the approval trail commissioned (Internal Audit or external). Terms of reference: process, not persons. | Group Internal Audit | Group GC, Group CMO |
| T+36 hrs | Regulator / ministry / ad-standards contact if tier requires (§14). Proactive, factual, low-key. | Market Corporate Affairs | Group GC |
| T+48 hrs | Cost envelope first estimate; revenue-at-risk range; materiality assessment initiated (§8). | Market Finance Lead + Group IR | CFO |
| T+72 hrs | Pod review against tripwires (§3). Confirm, escalate or de-escalate tier. Publish internal 72-hour note. | Pod chair | Regional President |

**Pre-drafted artefacts that must exist before the crisis, not during it** — see Annex B: three tiers of holding statement; internal all-employee note; retailer/distributor letter; customer-service and store FAQ; social response decision tree; spokesperson brief and hostile-question Q&A; monitoring cadence and dashboard definition; war-room roster across time zones; regulator briefing note.

---

## 2. Severity tiers

One response setting was a mistake. Under-reaction and over-reaction are both failure modes, and the second is the one organisations rarely admit to.

| | **Tier 1 — Social flare** | **Tier 2 — National story** | **Tier 3 — Institutional escalation** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Indicators** *(illustrative thresholds, to be calibrated to market size)* | <1,500 unique authors in 24 hrs; no mainstream pickup; no institutional contact; no safety concern | ≥2 national outlets; or >5,000 unique authors; or a statement by a recognised religious, cultural or political figure; or influencer withdrawal | Regulator, ministry or state media action; organised boycott with named sponsor; retailer delisting notice; criminal complaint; any safety incident |
| **Asset action** | Withdraw asset in-market; freeze scheduled activity | Full in-market withdrawal incl. POS, packaging, retail screens; global freeze; global withdrawal tested under §4 | Global withdrawal presumed unless §4 rule clearly excludes it |
| **Voice** | Written statement, Market Comms Lead named | Named Market GM, form per §9 overlay | Regional President or Group CEO, in-market presence |
| **Spend authority without further sign-off** | Up to 5% of in-market annual media budget *(illustrative)* | Up to 25% *(illustrative)* | Beyond ceiling: Group CFO decision within 4 hours, not 4 days |
| **Cadence** | Twice daily pod check | Pod on standing bridge, 4-hourly reporting | Continuous war room; daily Regional President briefing; Board Risk Committee informed within 48 hrs |
| **Government contact** | None | Prepared, held ready | Initiated proactively |

**Movement between tiers is by tripwire, not by feeling.** Any single Tier-2 indicator promotes the incident within one hour. De-escalation requires **two consecutive 24-hour periods** below the threshold *and* no open institutional item; it is proposed by the pod and confirmed by the Regional President, so that the decision to relax is a shared one rather than an individual's exposure.

---

## 3. Withdrawal decision rule (replacing the earlier instruction)

Withdraw **globally** where any of the following holds:

(a) the asset ran, in any form, outside the market;
(b) the offence **travels** — faith, race, historical atrocity, national dignity of a diaspora, disability, sexual violence;
(c) the asset is already circulating internationally in screenshot or re-upload form, such that withdrawal is news that has already broken;
(d) a global retailer, platform or partner has raised it.

Otherwise: **withdraw in-market, freeze globally, and hold** — with a re-test at each 24-hour pod review. A global withdrawal briefs markets that never saw the creative; it is a real action with real cost and should be chosen, not assumed.

**Who decides.** Withdrawal *in-market* is the market's to make, without consultation. Withdrawal *globally* exceeds any single market's authority and belongs to the Group CMO. To prevent this becoming a queue, the standing rule is: the market proposes; the Group CMO ratifies or overrides **within two hours**; absent a response, the market's proposal stands and is minuted as having done so. Speed is protected without anyone being asked to act outside their standing.

**Do not silently delete.** Leave a visible marker where the asset stood — "this content has been withdrawn; our response is here" — and link forward. Quiet deletion is read as concealment, and reasonably so.

---

## 4. Decision architecture

A crisis pod, formed within the hour, small enough to meet on one call.

| Seat | Role |
|---|---|
| **Market GM** *(chair)* | Holds the pen and the final call on tone. Accountable for the market. |
| **Local cultural counsel** — external, respected in-market | Reality-checks every draft. Right of veto on language and on apology form. |
| **Market Comms Lead** | Sequencing, channels, media relationships. |
| **Market Counsel**, supported by Group GC | Identifies specific exposure in writing (§7). |
| **Digital / Community Lead** | Real-time listening, comment governance, platform escalation. |
| **Market Sales Director** | Retail, distribution, franchise exposure. |
| **Security / HR representative** | Safety and welfare (§6). |
| **Group representative** (one person, senior) | Present to unblock, and to carry the market's position upward accurately. |

Two enabling conditions, and we would rather they be settled now, in calm, than negotiated under pressure:

- **A pre-authorised mandate letter**, signed in advance by the Group CEO and CFO, granting the pod authority within its tier to withdraw, spend to the ceiling, and publish an apology without further sign-off. This is not a reduction of hierarchy; it is hierarchy exercised early, so that the market team acts with visible senior backing rather than in advance of it. Colleagues will act quickly only if they are confident they are acting with permission.
- **Group functions hold consultation rights within tier, and decision rights only where the tier table says so.** Objections are logged in the incident log and answered within the day; they do not queue the response. Nothing is lost — the record is complete, and every view is preserved.

If the organisation is not, on reflection, willing to grant that mandate, that is an entirely legitimate position. The honest consequence is a slower response, and the strategy should then be sized to a slower response rather than pretending otherwise. Either is workable. The mixture is not.

---

## 5. Verifying the reaction before sizing the response

Within six hours the pod should have a written read on:

- **Scale**: unique authors vs. total mentions; reposts vs. original posts; follower-weighted reach.
- **Concentration**: in-market vs. diaspora vs. unrelated geographies.
- **Authenticity**: account age, posting velocity, template language, network clustering — indicators of coordinated amplification.
- **Sponsorship**: competitor, political, activist or state involvement.
- **Depth**: are people describing hurt, or describing us? The first requires apology; the second requires apology and structural answer.

This does not qualify the duty to apologise for genuine hurt. It determines *tier*, *voice* and *spend*. A national on-camera apology deployed against a small inauthentic cluster is not caution; it is the creation of a national story that did not exist.

---

## 6. Safety, welfare and duty of care

Placed before the communications sections deliberately. This was missing from the previous draft, and it should never have been.

- **Assessment within two hours**: offices, stores, warehouses, distribution vehicles, agency premises, employee commutes. Physical security uplift where indicated; remote working option offered, not imposed.
- **Community managers and customer-service staff** are the people absorbing the abuse. Rotate them on four-hour shifts, remove individual names from public-facing accounts, provide a supervisor on the line at all times, and open counselling access immediately rather than on request.
- **The named spokesperson becomes a personal target.** Before anyone is asked to appear: threat assessment, personal and family security review, social account lockdown, doxxing monitoring, and an explicit written undertaking that the company carries the consequences of the appearance. No one should be asked to step forward without that undertaking in hand.
- **Protest and boycott handling**: store-level protocol (do not engage, do not film, do not remove protestors, notify security), pre-agreed with retail partners.
- **Local nationals employed by us** may face social exposure their expatriate colleagues do not. Ask, individually and privately, before assuming anyone is comfortable being visible.
- **Legal-personal exposure**: where the market's law exposes the country manager personally (§7), that person does not sign, appear, or approve publications until Group GC has advised in writing and indemnity is confirmed.

---

## 7. Legal posture (rewritten)

The previous draft's "real but usually overstated — accept" was not a posture the working group was entitled to adopt on behalf of colleagues who carry the exposure. Corrected rule:

No revenue target, no cash requirement, no payback, no break-even, no unit economics. For an apparel expansion the omission of **working capital** is the most serious: two seasons of stock, factory minimums, sea-freight lead time and returns are the cash story, and a mid-sized balance sheet lives or dies on it. The paper asks a Board for "sight" while giving it nothing to size. As written, the CFO's first question ends the meeting.

---

## 2. A likely decision-reversing analytical error

**2.1 The India-vs-Türkiye cost comparison appears unmodelled, and may be backwards.**
The paper casts India as the margin/depth vector and Türkiye as a mere "hedge." But for goods sold into the EU:
- Türkiye enters **duty-free** under the customs union, with 3–5 week replenishment and low audit travel cost;
- India-made apparel generally pays **MFN duty in the ~12% band** (textiles having been graduated out of EU GSP benefits), plus 5–6 weeks of sea freight, plus the working capital that lead time consumes.

That is potentially a 15–20 point landed-cost swing against India before any FOB comparison. It should be verified with a customs adviser — the paper is right to caveat tariff readings — but the recommendation cannot rest on an unexamined assumption in the opposite direction. **On the face of it, the sequence should invert: Türkiye first (cheaper, faster, easier to audit, EU-compliance-native), India second and deeper.**

**2.2 The Japan duty position is missed, and it cuts against the "hinge."**
The **EU–Japan EPA** eliminates duty on qualifying EU-origin apparel into Japan — a material advantage for the beachhead that the paper doesn't claim, and a scoring error ("duty/logistics 3"). More importantly, **India-made goods do not qualify for EPA preference**, so the very stock produced by Vector B loses that advantage in Vector A. There may be a route via India–Japan CEPA shipping direct from India, but that is a different supply chain with different QC and inventory logic. The hinge is presented as a free option; it is not, and the origin arithmetic is where its value is decided.

---

## 3. Method and consistency problems

**3.1 §2 contradicts §1.** Having argued that demand and supply must not be forced onto one map, the paper then ranks Japan, India and Türkiye on a *single* weighted scorecard containing both demand and supply criteria. Japan scoring 1 on "supply fit" is not a finding; it is a category error. Two screens are needed.

**3.2 The scorecard shows no arithmetic.** Weights are given, scores are given, and the weighted total — the entire point — is omitted. The "Lean" column therefore appears asserted rather than derived, which invites the suspicion that the conclusion preceded the model.

**3.3 The USA reversibility score (2) is questionable.** Wholesale-only or specialist e-tail entry in the US is *more* reversible than a Japanese department-store and agent build. The greenwash litigation point is fair; the reversibility score looks bent to fit the conclusion.

**3.4 Two significant geographies are absent without explanation.** **Australia/New Zealand** — English-language, high sustainability willingness-to-pay, low friction, and **counter-seasonal**, which turns end-of-season EU stock from a markdown problem into a margin channel. For a mid-sized brand with inventory risk, that is a strategically distinctive option and its omission is a real gap. **Canada** and the **Nordics/CEE** deserve at least a line of dismissal.

**3.5 Bandwidth realism.** Three vectors across two continents in 0–18 months, with one named hire, in a mid-sized company. The claim that each vector "makes the others cheaper" is asserted and not demonstrated; on the evidence presented, A and B share almost no infrastructure in the first 18 months. Either justify the parallelism with a resourcing plan, or run Türkiye + Japan first and hold India to Gate 2.

---

## 4. Under-treated risks

- **Organic cotton certification fraud in India** is a documented, material, brand-lethal risk for a claims-led business. It is buried inside a "claim risk: 2" cell. It warrants its own workstream: transaction-certificate verification, isotope/DNA testing, unannounced audits, and a written position on what happens if a claim fails post-shipment.
- **Are we big enough to be a good customer?** No mention of whether our order volumes clear MOQs at quality Indian mills, or where we sit in a factory's priority order. This is the most common failure mode for mid-sized brands sourcing in Asia.
- **Türkiye macro:** FX and wage inflation in USD terms, energy costs, cotton import dependency. "Duty-free and fast" is true; "stable" is not automatic.
- **Japan specifics:** JPY weakness against a euro cost base, department-store concession economics (margin plus staffing), extreme quality/returns tolerance, Japanese-language service obligations, and a premium market that is deep but not growing.
- **The credibility of our own footprint.** A sustainability brand adding long-haul distribution and a third continent of production expands its Scope 3 while marketing itself on carbon. Air-freighted replenishment would be indefensible. Under CSRD this becomes disclosable, and under the EU Green Claims/Empowering Consumers regime it constrains language. Japan's own Keihyō-hō and the Consumer Affairs Agency greenwashing guidance also apply. None of this appears.
- **No competitor map at all.** Patagonia is formidable in Japan; the premium/quiet-quality space is contested by domestic players and by Muji's adjacency. Positioning claims in §5 cannot be assessed without knowing who already owns them.

---

## 5. Evidence and register

- Positioning claims ("Japan pays for longevity without being lectured", "vegan language performs in Korea") are plausible and unsourced. There is a cheap validation set the paper never asks for: **existing cross-border orders from Japan/Korea on the current EU site**, marketplace price/assortment scrapes, search volume, and 8–10 buyer interviews. Add a 60-day, low-cost validation phase and make Gate 1 contingent on it.
- The register is over-deferential and inherited from a different document. "This paper does not tell anyone what to do" is not humility, it is abdication — and it is inconsistent with a paper that makes a firm three-vector recommendation. Cut the apparatus, keep the caveats where they attach to specific numbers.
- **No ask.** State it: approve €X for a 60-day validation and trademark filings, decision at Gate 1 on [date].

---

## 6. Concrete fixes, in priority order

1. Finish the document: §§6–16

# International Expansion — Entry & Establishment Strategy
## Version 2 (complete; for Board decision at Gate 0)

**Company:** Mid-sized sustainable apparel brand, established in Western Europe
**Prepared by:** Growth working group, with Sourcing, Finance and Legal
**Circulated to:** CEO · CFO · Brand & Product Director · Sourcing Director · Head of Digital · Head of Legal · Head of Sustainability · Board

**Status.** A recommendation, with a specific ask (§16). Version 1 was reviewed and found to be an unfinished paper that answered one of the three questions asked, and that rested a sequencing decision on an unexamined duty assumption. Both criticisms were correct, and one of them reverses our recommendation. We are grateful for the correction; it is far cheaper here than at Gate 2.

**Figures marked *illustrative*** are shape, to be confirmed with Finance, a customs adviser and the market. They are given so the size of the commitment is visible, not because we are confident in them. **All duty and tariff positions in this paper are a strategic reading and require written confirmation from a customs adviser before Gate 1.**

---

## 0. What changed from Version 1, and why

We record this so colleagues who commented can see their guidance carried through.

| Change | Reason |
|---|---|
| **1. Sequence inverted: Türkiye is now the first supply move, India the second.** | The landed-cost arithmetic was not modelled. Türkiye enters the EU duty-free under the customs union; Indian apparel pays MFN duty in the ~12% band, with 5–6 weeks of sea freight and the working capital that consumes. That is a materially different answer, and it was ours to check before recommending. §3, §6. |
| **2. EU–Japan EPA now claimed, and the "hinge" re-priced.** | EU-origin goods enter Japan duty-free under the EPA. India-made goods do not qualify. The hinge was presented as a free option; the origin arithmetic decides its value. §6.3. |
| **3. Two screens, not one.** | Ranking Japan on "supply fit" was a category error against our own §1 argument. §2 now runs a demand screen and a supply screen separately, with the weighted arithmetic shown. |
| **4. A marketing plan now exists (§8), with channel splits, CAC/LTV assumptions and a trade calendar.** | Version 1 had four bullets. The brief asked for channels; we did not answer it. |
| **5. Operational steps now exist (§9), led by trademark filing in Month 0.** | Japan is first-to-file and apparel squatting is routine. Filing before any agent conversation, listing or press. Its absence was a straightforward error. |
| **6. Numbers (§11): revenue, working capital, unit economics, break-even, cash-at-risk.** | Asking the Board for sight while giving it nothing to size is not a modest paper, it is an unusable one. |
| **7. Australia/NZ added and seriously considered; Canada, Nordics/CEE, USA dismissed on the record.** | Counter-seasonality is a genuine inventory-risk answer for a brand our size. Its omission was a gap, not a judgement. |
| **8. Organic cotton certification integrity promoted to its own workstream (§10.1); competitor map added (§7); our own Scope 3 credibility addressed (§10.5).** | Each is brand-lethal for a claims-led business and each was buried in a scorecard cell. |
| **9. Register corrected.** | "This paper does not tell anyone what to do" was inherited from a crisis playbook and was abdication dressed as courtesy. This paper does recommend. Caveats now attach to specific numbers, where they belong. |

---

## 1. The question behind the question

The brief asks for one region delivering new customers *and* new manufacturing. That is two questions wearing one coat.

The geographies where premium sustainable apparel commands a price are, with few exceptions, not the geographies where it is competitively made. Forcing both onto one map produces a compromise that is second-best at each: a factory base in a market that cannot afford the product, or a demand beachhead with no supply logic behind it.

We therefore separate the vectors and look for where they *touch*:

- **Demand** — where are there latent buyers who will pay for the proposition?
- **Supply** — where can we make it better, more traceably, and with a second source we do not currently have?
- **The hinge** — is there a region where a supply base can, over time, also serve regional demand? "Make in region, sell in region" is where the margin sits and where the carbon story stops being a slide. §6.3 tests whether the hinge survives its own duty arithmetic.

**Our real starting asset.** We are single-sourced, EU-concentrated, and carrying a regulatory apparatus (CSRD, CSDDD, Green Claims / Empowering Consumers, ESPR and Digital Product Passport, textile EPR) that we have treated as cost. That apparatus is a traceability and substantiation capability almost no competitor in our size class has built. Our export may not be the clothing.

---

## 2. Screening — two screens, arithmetic shown

Version 1's single scorecard contradicted §1. Corrected: demand markets are screened on demand criteria, supply markets on supply criteria. Weights are chosen for a mid-sized balance sheet, i.e. weighted toward **reversibility**.

### 2.1 Demand screen

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Segment paying a premium for provenance/quality | 25% |
| Channel access for an unknown foreign brand | 20% |
| Reversibility of entry (wholesale/marketplace before entity) | 20% |
| Claim-substantiation and litigation risk (inverse) | 15% |
| Operating friction (entity, tax, labelling, payments, FX) | 10% |
| Inventory-risk relief (counter-seasonality, off-price channel) | 10% |

Scores 1–5, *illustrative*, weighted total to one decimal:

| Market | Premium 25% | Channel 20% | Revers. 20% | Claim risk 15% | Friction 10% | Inventory 10% | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Japan** | 5 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 2 | **4.05** |
| **Australia / NZ** | 4 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 4 | 5 | **4.15** |
| **South Korea** | 4 | 4 | 5 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **3.65** |
| **USA (East Coast)** | 4 | 2 | 4 | 2 | 3 | 2 | **3.10** |
| **Canada** | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 2 | **3.05** |
| **UAE / Gulf** | 3 | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3 | **3.45** |

Corrections we accept from review, visible in the numbers above: **Japan's duty position is a 4, not a 3** (EU–Japan EPA, §6.3). **The USA's reversibility is a 4, not a 2** — wholesale and specialist e-tail entry there is genuinely reversible, and Version 1's score was bent to fit its conclusion. The USA is still not first, but for the honest reasons: acquisition cost against a mature, well-funded domestic sustainable cohort, and a claims-litigation environment in a category of its own. That is a claim-risk argument, and it is now scored as one.

**Australia/NZ now scores marginally ahead of Japan** and was missing from Version 1 altogether. English-language, low friction, high willingness-to-pay, and — the point that matters for a brand carrying our inventory risk — **counter-seasonal**, which converts end-of-season European stock from a markdown problem into a full-margin channel. We do not, however, recommend it as the *beachhead* (§3), and the reason should be stated plainly rather than hidden in the scorecard: the market is shallow, it credentials us nowhere else, and a scorecard that rewards ease will always over-reward it. Judgement overrides the model here, and we would rather say so than adjust a weight until the model agrees with us. **Canada** is dismissed as a US derivative better entered after the US. **Nordics/CEE** is home-region deepening, not expansion, and belongs in the core plan.

### 2.2 Supply screen

| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Landed cost into EU (FOB + duty + freight + WC carry) | 30% |
| Capability at our quality and certification standard | 20% |
| Certification and claim integrity (verifiable chain of custody) | 20% |
| Speed / replenishment and audit accessibility | 15% |
| Country and FX stability | 10% |
| Headroom to grow with us; are we a good customer? | 5% |

| Source | Landed 30% | Capability 20% | Integrity 20% | Speed 15% | Stability 10% | Headroom 5% | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Türkiye** | 5 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 2 | 3 | **4.30** |
| **India** | 3 | 5 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 5 | **3.25** |
| **Portugal (incumbent-adjacent)** | 3 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 2 | **4.15** |
| **Vietnam** | 4 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 4 | 2 | **3.70** |
| **Bangladesh** | 5 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 4 | **3.35** |

**This is the reversal.** Türkiye's landed-cost score is not a preference, it is the customs union: duty-free entry, 3–5 week replenishment, GOTS-certified capacity, and a two-hour flight for unannounced audits. India's capability and headroom are the best on the board — fibre-to-garment depth, artisan capability that is defensible as *product* rather than as story — but it carries ~12% MFN duty into the EU, 5–6 weeks of sea freight, the working capital that lead time consumes, and the certification-integrity exposure in §10.1. Version 1 called Türkiye a "hedge." On the arithmetic it is the first move.

**Bangladesh** scores best on cost and worst where we cannot afford to score badly. The LDC graduation timetable removes the duty advantage inside our planning horizon, and it substitutes one single-country concentration for another.

**Portugal** is included deliberately, and it scores second. Before we cross a continent, the Board is entitled to ask whether deepening and diversifying within our existing supply geography answers the sourcing half of the brief at a fraction of the risk. Our answer is that it answers resilience but not cost or growth headroom — but it is a legitimate alternative to the whole of Vector B, and §15 treats it as one.

---

## 3. The recommendation — three vectors, re-sequenced

| Vector | Where | Why | Horizon |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Demand beachhead** | **Japan**, Tokyo-first | Pays for material quality, longevity and repair without needing to be lectured. Wholesale and department-store structures let an unknown brand be validated by an intermediary the customer already trusts. **EU-origin goods enter duty-free under the EPA.** Deep, patient, and it credentials us across Asia. | Months 0–18 |
| **B1 — Supply, first move** | **Türkiye** (Aegean/İzmir, İstanbul) | Duty-free into the EU, 3–5 week replenishment, GOTS capacity, auditable on a two-hour flight. **Cheaper landed, faster, and EU-compliance-native.** Learn second-sourcing here, where mistakes are recoverable. | Months 0–12 |
| **B2 — Supply, deeper** | **India** — knits Tiruppur/Coimbatore, wovens Bengaluru/NCR, artisan Rajasthan/Gujarat | Fibre-to-garment depth, growth headroom, and craft capability that becomes product. Held to **Gate 2**, conditional on the certification-integrity workstream (§10.1) passing and on our order book clearing quality-mill MOQs (§10.2). | Months 12–30 |
| **Counter-seasonal channel** | **Australia / NZ**, wholesale-only | Not a beachhead — an inventory instrument. Two agents, no entity, no marketing spend, taking EU end-of-season at full local margin. Cheap, reversible, and it funds part of Vector A. | Months 6–18 |
| **The hinge** | India, later, **only if §6.3 clears** | India-made, Asia-sold. Shortest freight, cleanest carbon arithmetic we will ever have — but India-origin goods forfeit EPA preference into Japan. We buy the option only when the origin arithmetic is written down. | Month 30+ |

**Why this sequence and not Version 1's.** A generates price validation and the story; B1 generates margin, speed and a second source immediately and cheaply; the Australian channel absorbs inventory risk that would otherwise sit against A's launch; B2 is the growth engine, entered once we know how to run a second source at all. Version 1 ran A and B(India) in parallel and asserted they made each other cheaper. On the evidence they share almost no infrastructure in the first eighteen months, and the assertion was unearned. Türkiye and Japan *do* share something real: both are served by the same EU-origin production base, and EPA preference depends on it.

**Bandwidth.** Three moves, one continent-crossing deferred. The resourcing plan is in §11.4. If the honest answer at Gate 0 is that we have capacity for two moves rather than three, drop the Australian channel — it is the most reversible and the least strategic. Do not drop B1, and do not accelerate B2 to compensate.

---

## 4. Entry mode — light footprint, high learning

Distributor versus subsidiary is a question of *stage*, not philosophy.

**Japan, Phase 1 (Months 0–12).**
- **Commercial agent, not exclusive distributor.** Commission-remunerated; exclusivity limited to 12 months and to named accounts; performance-linked renewal. Exclusivity given away cheaply in month two is how brands lose a decade in Japan.
- **Marketplace in parallel** — ZOZOTOWN and/or Rakuten Fashion for demand signal and size-curve data. Commission is material (*illustrative: 25–35%*). Treat as paid research with revenue attached, not as the channel.
- **Own D2C** properly localised: Japanese-language site, JPY pricing, credit/konbini/PayPay/Rakuten Pay, domestic returns address, **LINE as primary CRM** rather than email.
- **One hire before any of it**: a senior, local Japan Market Lead with a wholesale rolodex. One excellent person and no office beats an office and a coordinator.

**Japan, Phase 2 (from Gate 2).** *Kabushiki Kaisha* or branch; 3PL in Chiba/Kanagawa; a controlled pop-up or shop-in-shop before any lease. Tokyo physical retail is a marketing instrument with a rent bill — bought when the brand can fill it, not to make the brand exist.

**Türkiye (supply).** Direct vendor relationships from the outset; no agent. Two mills minimum per product family. A retained local QC/compliance inspector (part-time, *illustrative €3–4k/month*) rather than an office. Written FOB pricing in EUR, not USD, to keep FX exposure where we can see it.

**India (from Gate 2).** Buying agent for months 0–9 of that phase to compress the search, replaced by our **own sourcing liaison office** by month 12 — the agent's incentive is order volume, ours is chain-of-custody integrity, and those diverge quietly.

**Australia/NZ.** Two commission agents, wholesale-only, no entity, no local stockholding beyond consignment. If it fails, it costs a season of samples.

**What we avoid.** A JV we do not need for market access; a licence that puts our name on product we do not control; an acquisition of a local brand before we can value it.

---

## 5. Product positioning

"Sustainable" does not translate. It localises, or it fails. **These claims are our working hypotheses, not findings — Gate 1 is contingent on the validation in §12.1 testing them.**

| Market | What the proposition is *about* | What to keep quiet |
|---|---|---|
| **Western Europe (home)** | Certified, circular, transparent — an ethical purchase | — |
| **Japan** | **Longevity, material honesty, quiet craft.** Fabric weight, seam construction, repair service, "one you keep for ten years". Environmental credentials as *evidence of care* — in the footnote, not the headline. | Moralising. Loud activism. Volume claims about CO₂ saved: immodest, and it invites verification we may not survive. |
| **Australia / NZ** | Durability for an outdoor climate; provenance stated plainly | European superiority of any kind |
| **South Korea (wave 2)** | **Design credibility with a conscience attached.** Silhouette first, story second, social proof throughout. | Slow-fashion sermons in a market moving in six-week cycles. |
| **Gulf (watch)** | Quality, modest-adaptable cut, discretion | Lifestyle instruction |

**Product architecture — 70/20/10.**
- **70% carry-over core**, unchanged: protects margin and brand coherence.
- **20% regional adaptation** — the unglamorous work: sizing down one to two increments with revised sleeve and inseam for Japan; lighter fabric weights for humid summers; a rainy-season capsule; colour palettes reset from Northern European reference; layering logic instead of coat logic.
- **10% regional exclusive** — capsule pieces using India's artisan capability, sold only in Asia. Deferred with B2 to Gate 2; it is where the hinge quietly begins.

**Price.** Position at or slightly above the local premium-contemporary band. Do not import EU price lists with a currency conversion attached. Landed cost, duty, agent commission and marketplace commission must all sit *inside* the price before it is published — see §11.2, where they visibly do not at current EU RRP, which is why Japanese RRP is set at +18%.

---

## 6. Duty, origin and landed cost — the arithmetic the last draft skipped

*All figures illustrative and subject to written customs advice.*

### 6.1 Into the EU

| Source | Duty | Freight | Lead time | WC carry effect | Indicative landed index (Portugal = 100) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Portugal (incumbent) | 0% | Road | 2–3 wks | Low | **100** |
| **Türkiye** | **0% (customs union)** | Road/short sea | 3–5 wks | Low | **88** |
| India | **~12% MFN** (textiles graduated from GSP) | Sea | 5–6 wks + inland | High | **94** |
| Bangladesh | 0% (EBA, until graduation) | Sea | 6–8 wks | High | **84, falling to ~96 post-graduation** |

The Türkiye/India gap is the paper's central correction: on these assumptions India's FOB advantage is consumed by duty, freight and lead-time capital before it reaches a European warehouse. India earns its place on capability, craft and headroom — not on cost — and it should be argued for on those grounds or not at all.

### 6.2 Into Japan

**EU–Japan EPA eliminates duty on qualifying EU-origin apparel.** This is a real advantage and Version 1 failed to claim it. Requirements: origin criteria satisfied, self-certification via statement on origin, supplier declarations retained, and — the operational point — **records held for the retention period and auditable**. Türkiye-made goods do **not** carry EU origin for EPA purposes. Japanese-market stock in Phase 1 should therefore be **EU-produced**, and this constraint must be visible to Sourcing before it makes allocation decisions. It also means Türkiye's cost advantage applies to European sales, not Japanese ones.

### 6.3 The hinge, re-priced

India-made goods forfeit EPA preference into Japan. India–Japan CEPA offers a route, but only shipping **direct from India** — a different supply chain, different QC presence, different inventory logic, and a duty position to be confirmed line by line. The hinge is therefore **not a free option**. It costs: a second Japanese inventory pool, a second origin-documentation regime, and QC capability in India serving a market our Indian team will never see. We propose one thing only at this stage: **do not close it** — write India–Japan CEPA classification into the Gate 2 terms of reference and price it there.

---

## 7. Competitor map — who already owns the words we want

Positioning cannot be assessed in a vacuum. Version 1 had none of this.

| Japan | Position held | Implication for us |
|---|---|---|
| **Patagonia Japan** | Formidable; owns activist-environmental credibility and repair | Do not contest activism. Contest *quiet* craft. |
| **Muji (adjacency)** | Owns restraint, material honesty, everyday price | We must be visibly *better made*, not merely plainer. Restraint alone is taken. |
| **Domestic mid-premium (e.g. established Japanese makers, mill-brands)** | Own fabric provenance and construction narrative on home ground | Our edge is verified chain of custody and European construction, not "we care about fabric" |
| **Global contemporary premium** | Own newness and store presence | We do not compete on newness. Carry-over is our position, not our limitation. |

**Consequence for §5.** "Longevity and material honesty" is contested territory in Japan, not open ground. Our differentiator must be the *verifiable* part — the traceability apparatus built for CSRD/DPP, which domestic mill-brands assert but rarely document. That is a narrower and more defensible claim than Version 1 made, and it should be tested in the buyer interviews at §12.1.

---

## 8. Marketing channels — the section the brief asked for and Version 1 did not deliver

### 8.1 Japan channel architecture and role

| Channel | Role | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Wholesale — select boutiques, then department-store shop-in-shop** | Credentialing | The customer trusts the retailer before us. Target 12–20 doors by Month 18. Department-store concession economics are punishing (margin *plus* staffing) — enter only from Gate 2. |
| **Trade calendar** | Buyer access | **Rooms (Feb/Sep)**, **Plug-In**, plus a Tokyo **showroom agency** retained seasonally. Showroom representation is how Japanese wholesale actually works; skipping it means cold-calling buyers who do not buy cold. |
| **Marketplaces — ZOZOTOWN, Rakuten Fashion** | Demand signal, size curve, discovery | ZOZO for fashion discovery and fit data (ZOZOSUIT-era size norms); Rakuten for point-economy shoppers and search reach; Amazon JP deferred — it is a price-led environment and poor for brand construction. |
| **Own D2C (Shopify Markets Pro or equivalent)** | Margin, data, CRM | Japanese-language, JPY, local payments, domestic returns. Target only ~20% of Year-1 revenue; D2C-first in Japan without a known brand is expensive. |
| **LINE** | Primary CRM | Official account + rich menu; LINE, not email. Broadcast discipline: two messages/month maximum. |
| **Earned media / PR** | Credibility | Retained Tokyo PR (*illustrative ¥400–600k/month*). Targets: Fudge, Ginza, Casa Brutus adjacency, Business of Fashion Japan, WWD Japan. Angle: European mill provenance and repair service, **not** sustainability advocacy. |
